Oscilloscope
How this works
  • Rest the pointer on any control and the line in the Picture section, along the bottom, says what it does; More, or ?, opens a card with what is moving it and the controls either side. Settings → This window turns the line off.
  • An oscilloscope draws what a signal is doing. Three ways of drawing it, and the switch marked Display chooses.
  • Y–T is the waveform Amplitude up, time across. Timebase sets how much time is on screen, in the 1–2–5 steps a scope has always stepped in.
  • X–Y plots one channel against the other Time is thrown away. Two tones of the same frequency draw a line, an ellipse or a circle depending only on the angle between them; simple ratios close into figures.
  • One input has no second axis — so lag makes one A single instrument down a single input gives two identical channels, and identical channels draw a diagonal line and nothing else, whatever the preset. Lag X–Y, on the Bench under Picture → Vertical, plots the signal against itself a moment earlier instead. A held note becomes a closed loop whose shape is its harmonic content, and it moves when you move.

    This is a phase portrait, not a Lissajous figure: the second axis is the same signal, so what you are reading is how the sound changes over that moment rather than how two sounds relate. Auto sets the delay to a quarter of a period, which is what makes a pure tone a circle, and it locks slowly on purpose — chasing the pitch would hold the circle round through vibrato and hide the very thing worth seeing. Locked slowly, vibrato makes the loop turn.

    Heard is how much of the delayed copy reaches the right speaker, when the speakers are on the shaped side. Heard, a signal plus itself a moment later is a comb filter that tracks the pitch. In headphones it cuts deepest at half, and in a room at full. It starts at 20%, which is mostly width, and stops at 50% — the top of the knob is the setting where, in headphones, the right ear loses some of a note's harmonics entirely. That is allowed on purpose; it is where the effect is strongest.
  • AC coupling, and where its corner sits Under Vertical, per lane. It blocks what is not moving, so a converter with a DC offset does not push the trace off the screen — a one-pole high pass, the same one a bench scope puts in front of its input. The corner is where it starts taking things away: at ten hertz, which is where a scope usually sits, a slow drift goes and the signal does not; down at one hertz almost nothing is removed quickly, which is what you want when the drift IS the signal; up at twenty it thins the bottom of a bass note as well.

    The corner is worth knowing about because the numbers under the trace are about the coupled signal, not the raw one. At ten hertz that moves a peak reading by a per cent or two, and rather more on anything near the corner; at one hertz an asymmetric signal — a half-wave rectified tone, say — can read a third higher, because a pole that slow has not finished taking the offset out within the window. That is what AC coupling at one hertz means rather than a fault, and the readout names the corner while it is on so the numbers say which signal they are about.

    The same corner reaches the speakers when they are on the shaped side, from one set of numbers: the screen and the speakers cannot disagree about what AC coupling is.
  • Spect is a spectrogram Frequency up, time running right to left, level as ink. Hover it and it names the frequency and the note under the pointer.
  • Zoom magnifies, and the wheel works In Y–T it shows a slice of the capture stretched, centred on the trigger — the record is unchanged, so the measurements still read all of it. In X–Y it scales the figure; on the spectrogram it closes in the frequency band.
  • A filter, on two taps Under Filter. It reshapes the trace, which is the point of having one here: a low pass rounds a square's corners toward a sine, a notch carves a harmonic out of the picture, a resonant sweep draws its own ringing. Screen reads and Speakers get are separate switches, so the filter can be an instrument for looking while what you hear is untouched, or both, or the other way round. Resonance is nought for gentle and a hundred for extreme, and at nought a low pass is maximally flat. It runs on the samples rather than in the audio graph, so it reaches the test tone too — which is arithmetic and has no audio graph at all. Point a source at the cutoff and it sweeps.
  • The voice: a second oscillator inside it Under Oscillator, on the Ink tab. A second oscillator runs at Ratio times the note, and FM swings the voice's phase with it: pure at nought, then brighter, then bells and clangour. A 3:2 ratio sounds harmonic for the same reason a 3:2 figure closes. Ring multiplies by it instead and takes the note away. Sync runs a saw or square faster than the note and restarts it every note cycle, so the pitch holds while the tone tears; put an LFO or the envelope on it for the classic sweep. Sub adds a square or sine an octave or two down, and Unison stacks detuned copies so the figure thickens and shimmers. Warp bends the wave at the point of its cycle Warp at names: up pinches it there, down swells it, and either way the figure bulges where you put it and the tone brightens, still in tune. At nought it is off and the voice is exactly what it was. You can also set both by taking hold of the figure itself: see Warp the figure by hand. FM, Sync, Warp and Warp at can take sources. (It was called Bend until pitch bend came, 6 Nov.) With a split, it is the layer being edited, so the two halves of the keyboard can be two different voices. Nothing gets louder: copies and the sub are mixed, not piled up.
  • Warp the figure by hand In X–Y, the pointer turns to a hand near the figure. Take hold and pull, and the figure bends where you took hold: Warp at goes to that moment of the cycle and Warp to whatever brings the figure nearest your hand, so the sound changes as the picture does. They are the same two knobs, turned as your hand would turn them, and they stay where you let go; a gold ring marks the moment you have hold of, filled while the pull is bending the figure towards your hand and faint while no bend can. Double-click the figure to put the bend off. The bend moves the wave in time, never in level, and the figure stays on its centre, so it cannot be pulled out past its own edges: on a circle's diagonals it pinches inward either way, at its ends it reaches further on one side, a straight line only slides along itself, and a pull it cannot follow does nothing but say so. On a chord it follows roughly, since each note bends in its own cycle. With a split, the figure you take hold of is the layer you bend, and the panel goes to it. A press away from the figure, the photocell's reticle and drawing on the screen are left as they were, and on a phone a finger on the figure bends it rather than scrolling the page.
  • Shaping: drive, fold and crush, in every note Under Shaping, on the Ink tab. Drive pushes the wave into a soft ceiling, so a sine rounds towards a square; the reading is how much the quiet parts are lifted. Fold bends the wave back on itself each time it would pass full scale: the peaks fold into the wave, and in X–Y the figure grows petals. Put an LFO on it and they open and close. Crush takes the wave down to a few levels and Rate holds each sample, for the steps and the folding-back of a lo-fi sampler. It is done to each note on its own, before its envelope, so a chord stays a chord rather than turning to mud, and a note keeps its colour as it dies away. Behind the ⋯, four times oversampling is cleaner for a hard drive on a high note, and costs twice as much, so a big chord gives it up first; see The voice budget.
  • The voice filter: one in every note Under Voice filter, on the Play tab. A low, band or high pass or a notch in each note, after its shaping and before its level. Key track makes the cutoff follow the note, so a high note is not duller than a low one. Envelope sweeps the cutoff up or down by that many octaves with the filter's own envelope, whose four are behind the ⋯: a note that opens bright and closes, or a resonant wah, per note. The cutoff can take a source. The Filter on the Picture tab is a different thing: it filters the whole trace, for looking.
  • The voice budget: what a big chord gives up Every copy, every shaped note and every filter costs the computer something, and sixteen notes with everything turned up would cost more than it has — the sound would break up. So the page keeps a budget, and when a chord would go over it gives things up in the order they are missed least: first the four times oversampling for twice, then unison copies, then notes still fading after you let go, and only then held notes you cannot see — the inner voices of a chord, before any drawn one, and never the last note. A note given up fades out rather than clicking and stays silent until you lift its key. The readout says voice budget: and what it took, and the copies come back when you play the next chord or change what you asked for. No preset gets near it with eight notes on each layer; it is for patches built with everything on, and chords struck over long releases.
  • The plane: what folds the picture folds the sound The first module in the rack, on the Space & Memory tab, for the generator and for a microphone or a line input. Its Turn is the screen's rotation, which on a stereo pair turns the sound with the figure: turning a picture and turning a stereo image are the same matrix. Mirror folds the figure onto one half of itself, X onto its right or Y onto its top, and to the ear that is full-wave rectification, the octave-up pedal: a mirrored sine is its octave, every harmonic even. Radial is what happens at the circle: Clip rounds the loud parts off towards it, keeping every point's direction, so it is a clipper that does not bend the stereo image; Fold reflects them back in, a wavefolder on both channels at once. The radius can take a source; its knob is marked at 0.2, where the clip is quieter and distorted in a way worth keeping, and two taps on it land there. Twist turns each point by an angle in proportion to its distance from the middle, so the loud parts swirl and the quiet ones stay put — a stereo rotation that depends on level, and it can take a source too. Snap puts both channels on a grid, at six bits or five: a bitcrusher, and pixels. (A kaleidoscope, and coarser grids, went on 7 November: one sounded harsh whatever it drew, the others silent or harsh.) Under the module's arrow, Scale X and Scale Y are balance and width, and Shear leaks one channel into the other. All of it acts on what is drawn and on what is heard, and in poly on the chord you hear as well as the notes that are drawn.

    With two layers playing, Layers at the top of the section chooses. Together is one plane for both. A or B gives layer B a plane of its own, starting as a copy of A's, and says which layer's the controls are showing — the same choice as Edit A and B on the Play tab. B's has a Turn of its own, which can take a source like the screen's rotation can — an oscillator on it spins B alone — and while it does the Plane's own Turn turns layer A only, so one figure can stand still while the other turns. The picture does not move when you leave Together, but the sound does: each layer is now bent on its own, and a mirror on two chords apart is not a mirror on the two together, which also makes their difference tones. B's own is its phaser, chorus and delay too: the Delay module has the same Layers row, the same switch, and with B's shown its controls are B's, so one layer can echo while the other stays dry, or each at its own time. Only the oversampling stays one for both.

    The bending ones run at twice the sample rate, so that what they add above half the rate is filtered away rather than folded back as notes that are nowhere in the key. At 4 kHz the clip's worst stray tone is 27 dB down at once, 55 at twice and 108 at four times. The fold and the snap are rougher at any rate, which is their character. Under the module's arrow you can choose once or four times. While any of them is on, the picture and sound are 0.7 ms later; scale and shear cost nothing. A mirrored wave sits above zero, and AC coupling takes that off what you hear.

    On a microphone or a line input the plane works on what comes in, before anything draws it or plays it: what you see is what a monitored line input sends to the speakers. A mono input becomes two lanes while an effect is on, because what the effect makes of it is a pair. A band split does not get it: its lanes are not one stereo pair. The line beside the rack's title says which it is doing.
  • Phaser, chorus and delay: echoes you can see The rack's next three modules, on the Space & Memory tab, after the plane: the phaser, the chorus, then the delay, on a live input as well as the generator. Each one's Mix is how much of it you hear, and the delay's is how loud the repeats are, nought for off; Time is free, or Sync sets it to a note value of the tempo and it follows the tempo when that moves. Feedback brings each repeat back again, and stops at 0.9 so it always dies away. Ping-pong sends each repeat to the other side, so on the screen the ghost figures alternate between the figure and its mirror image across the diagonal. Chorus is a short delay whose time swings, one side on a sine and the other on its cosine, so the figure breathes and turns; with Feedback under its arrow it is a flanger. The delay's Mix and Time can take a source: on the mix, a pedal or a wheel brings repeats in from none, and the delay keeps listening while it is at nought, so what comes back is what you just played; on the time, a source stretches it an octave either way, and the repeats bend in pitch as it moves, like tape. Neither feedback can take one: a loop inside a loop is how a patch runs away. With two layers playing, the Delay module's Layers row gives layer B a phaser, a chorus and a delay of its own, with its plane — one switch for both — and a source on the delay's mix reaches each layer through that layer's own fade.

    Phaser turns each harmonic of the pair by a different amount — the low ones a little, the high ones nearly a whole turn — and sweeps where it turns them at Sweep, one channel on a sine and the other on its cosine. That is what it does to the picture: a line opens into a loop that widens and closes as the sweep goes round, and a figure twists unevenly, which nothing else on the tab does. Mixed with the dry pair it is the classic phaser's two moving notches. Range is how far it sweeps, up to two and a half octaves either side of 700 Hz, and under its arrow Resonance feeds it back on itself to sharpen the notches, stopping at 0.75 so it never rings on for ever. By default it comes before the chorus and the delay, so their copies are of the phased pair. Its amount can take a source, and the picture's Memory is on it by default: a picture that has stopped moving is phased until it goes somewhere new. In a plugin it is the host's eighth knob.
  • The picture as a score Tick Play the picture, under Score on the Picture tab, and a playhead crosses the screen at the tempo, playing what it passes. Low on the screen is low in pitch, in the page's key, over the octaves you choose; the brightest points in each column are the notes, up to four at once, and the brighter the harder. Draw a figure and it plays itself; turn it and the melody inverts. A long persistence is a score that lingers. The notes are heard in the generator's voice while it is heard, and never drawn, so the score cannot play itself into what it is reading. The playhead is on the page's bar, so its first column is always a downbeat and Stop under Key and tempo silences it; see below.
  • The arpeggiator Arp, in the Perform menu in the header, plays a held chord a note at a time at the tempo: up, down, up and back, in the order you played it, or at random, from a crotchet to a semiquaver triplet, over one to three octaves. In the dyad each step pairs your lowest note with the next, so the figure steps through the shapes of the chord's intervals in time. Every note is struck afresh, and the first waits a moment for the rest of the chord. Letting go stops it; switching it off with keys down gives the generator the whole chord. Its notes go out through MIDI out.
  • MIDI out Under Settings, MIDI, choose a port and a channel, and the score's notes go out to it. With a synth on Local Off the picture plays it, and its line outs coming back in close the loop through a real instrument. At most forty notes a second; every note is ended when the scope stops, the page is hidden, or the port changes; the readout says sending while they go.
  • Your input, into the generator Under Input into the generator, in Settings: your microphone or line input fed into the generator itself. FM bends the waveform's pitch with yours, faster and slower within every cycle you play. Ride scales the figure by it, so the sound rides on its outline. Clock plays the generator at your pitch, locked to each of your cycles, and a fifth or an octave above it if the interval says so. When you stop, it goes back to its own. It works on the test tone once its sound has started — a press anywhere starts it — and the line under the title says when it is not reaching it.
  • Persistence is the phosphor How slowly the screen forgets. Off for a waveform; long or infinite for X–Y, where the figure is built up a pass at a time. It is one knob, in the Picture section along the bottom: how long a stroke takes to fade to half, from off at the bottom to infinite at the top.
  • The picture plays the sound, always Whatever is drawn is read back and moves the sound, with nothing to route. There are three reads of the screen: Glow, how much of it is lit; Motion, how much the picture has just moved; and Memory, which climbs while the picture keeps coming back to where it has been — held still, or going round the same loop — and drains once it goes somewhere new. Glow folds the sound, Motion echoes it, and Memory twists the figure and turns the right channel's phase — which moves the picture, and so lets itself go. Glow and Motion are each measured against what the picture has been doing lately, so a figure that only ever lights a fifth of the screen still swings them right across; a picture held still reads nought, rather than having its tremble stretched into a swing.

    The Amount, first in the Picture section along the bottom, is how much. At nought it is an ordinary synthesiser, and the three meters at the section's end show what each read is doing; the name of each control the picture is moving lights up with how far it is moving it. Every preset sets it as part of its sound — the Settled ones, and the plain sine the page opens on, at nought — and from there it is yours, and it is on a pedal: a keyboard's expression pedal (the Nord's swell, controller 11) sets it. The reads live under the same rules as the photocell below: on any one control they share its half with the photocell and with anything you route from the picture yourself.

    Split into two sounds, each layer's figure is also a picture of its own, read on its own, and Pictures, in the Picture section's Advanced under What Scan reads, says whose sound each moves: A → A and B → B to start, each picture its own sound's; A → B to send A's picture to the other sound; both to send it to both. A sound that hears two pictures takes their average, so it is never pushed harder than by one. When the two pictures move each other's sounds, either one running away reins in the crossing as well as itself, so the pair cannot chase itself up. The site's compiled instrument and the plugin do all of this, as ?brain=js does.
  • Scan: the screen read back as the wave Under Scan, on the Picture tab. Sixty times a second the light on the screen is read round a circle beside the figure, and the reading becomes one cycle of the voice's wave, played at the note you hold, so the picture can change the timbre and never the pitch. Each reading fades into the next across its sixtieth of a second, and that step is part of the sound. Depth is how much of the voice it is; at the top a fifth of the shape stays under it, so the note keeps its pitch even on a picture whose strongest harmonic is not the first. A picture that moves is a wave that moves: a turning fifth thickens and thins as it turns. A still picture is a still wave, an ordinary tone. Softness blurs the light before it is read, three cells to start; at nought the thin lines read as spikes and buzz. Persistence beside them is the screen's, in seconds. The wave is evened to the same peak every reading, so the picture cannot make it louder; a circle through darkness keeps the last wave rather than reading nothing; and while the loop is running away its depth is reined in to a quarter, as the picture's own reads are. With a split, Depth is the layer being edited and each layer reads its own figure. The site's instrument and the plugin read their own screen sixty times a second of the sound, so there it is the same on any display; the page's own brain (?brain=js) reads the screen as it is drawn, and plays the latest reading at the same ticks.
  • Notes strike the screen; each hand reads the other's picture Strike, under Scan: every note you play lays a short arc of light on the circle Scan reads, as bright as you played it times the Strike amount, at the note's own place round the circle — C where the reading starts, each semitone a twelfth further round — so a chord strikes several places and a harder note moves the timbre further. Not always brighter: where the circle crossed bright lines the arc smooths them over. The light is like any other on the screen and fades by its Persistence, so with a long one a run of notes builds up and dies away. It is laid only where Scan is on, and at nought nothing is laid at all. The picture's meters see it, and struck hard and fast enough to fill the screen the loop is reined in as it would be for any picture running away.

    Reads, under Scan while a split draws a figure for each hand: what each layer's Scan reads — its own picture, the other layer's, or both averaged. Crossed, your left hand's wave is your right hand's figure and the right's is the left's; the two loops feed each other, so both are reined in together when either runs away.

    Hold the sustain pedal (or Pedal on the screen's keys) and a chord goes on sounding after you let go, with the loop still changing it. Stop holds the screen, which holds the tone still; Depth at nought takes Scan out. Strike and Reads play everywhere Scan does: on the site's instrument and in the plugin the strike is laid on the screen the instrument draws itself, and on the page's own brain on the screen you see.
  • Loop: seeing where Scan reads Loop, behind the Picture section's Advanced, draws the loop over the picture while you make a sound: a dashed ring where Scan is reading the screen (in X–Y, in each layer's own colour, on whichever picture that layer reads — crossed hands put each ring on the other figure), a dot on it where the voice was in its cycle when the table last changed, the table it is playing as a small waveform in the screen's corner, and the picture's verdict as a badge — the same word as the readout, in rust when the loop is running away. The dot is a stroboscope: it is sampled sixty times a second, so it stands still on a note at a multiple of 60 Hz and turns slowly otherwise. The ring follows the figure over about a second. Nothing appears until Scan is on; nothing is drawn on the spectrogram, and in Y–T only the table and the badge. It is drawn over the screen and never into it, so it cannot change what Scan reads or what you hear. Your choice is remembered on this browser and is never part of a setup.
  • The photocell: the picture moving the controls The Photocell card, in the modulation row, puts a light sensor on the screen: switch it On in its editor, or drag the card onto a knob, which switches it on. Drag the reticle onto the picture, or give it focus and move it a cell at a time with the arrow keys. How bright the phosphor is under it becomes a source, Photocell, which can be put on a control like an LFO: park it on the edge of a figure and it pulses as the beam sweeps past, drop it inside a filled figure and it reads how dense it is. Point it at rotation or zoom and the figure moves itself — and moves what the photocell sees, which is the loop. It fills with its own reading, so you can see what it is seeing. A loop needs its reticle on the trace of the figure at rest: in the dark it reads nought, nought moves nothing, and nothing ever lights it. So switching it on lands the reticle on the nearest bright part of the figure, if it is not on one already.

    It can reach any control, the filter and the generator included, so the picture can be heard as well as seen. Three things keep that loop from running away. It moves a control at most half as far as another source could, and every source reading the picture on one control shares that half between them — three of them on the cutoff move it no further than one. Its reading can change no faster than two full swings a second, so it cannot flip back and forth every frame. And the limiter is still last, so a loop that finds a resonance is caught rather than heard at full scale. Persistence is its memory: long persistence makes it slow and smooth, short makes it twitchy. Over a spectrogram it reads nothing, because no beam draws one. Clear, above the screen, wipes the screen and what the photocell sees, and leaves persistence as it was set.
  • What the picture says, and what the loop is doing Five more sources read the whole picture rather than one point, under the same rules, and are there whether or not the photocell is on. Roundness is one for a circle and nought for a line — and one for a square too, because it sees how spread a figure is, not its corners. Coverage is how much of the screen is lit. Change is how much the picture moved since the last frame. Novelty is how far the picture is from anything it showed in the last fifteen seconds: nought when it keeps coming back, high when it has gone somewhere new. Direction is which way round the beam travels, plus or minus. Boredom climbs slowly while the picture neither moves nor goes anywhere new, and drains once it does: put it on something that shakes the figure and a loop that has settled will, after a few seconds, nudge itself out again. It reaches less than the others and can never climb faster than a quarter a second.

    The readout says what the loop is doing: settled when nothing moves, cycling when it keeps coming back to where it has been, wandering when it moves and does not repeat, running away when the screen fills or the limiter is working hard to hold the sound down. Running away also reins the loop in: the picture stage's push falls to a quarter of itself over a second and a half, its bars turn rust while it is held, and it comes back slowly once the loop settles. The interesting setups are the wandering ones: two sources crossed onto two controls — say Roundness on the lag, with lag X–Y on, and Novelty on rotation — and persistence long enough to give it memory.
  • The beam has a brightness On a cathode-ray tube the spot's brightness is how long it dwelt on a spot, which means it goes as one over its speed. The trace turns bright where it slows to turn around and faint through the fast sweeps — which is most of why a real scope does not look like a plot. A circle comes out perfectly even, because a circle traced at a steady rate really does have constant speed.
  • Where it applies Picture → Advanced → Beam, with what only changes the look. On for X–Y, and off for the waveform by default: dimming the steep edge of a square wave fights the measuring that Y–T is for. Off / subtle / moderate / high widens both the range of tone and how much speed it takes to cross it. On a very long timebase the waveform falls back to a flat trace, because past two samples a pixel the screen is showing each column's range rather than a path, and a range has no speed.
  • Panes The goniometer, spectrum, harmonics and tuner, chosen in the Picture section's Advanced and shown beside the screen in Enlarge, with Picture only off. Turn them all off and the trace takes the whole width.
  • Enlarge The square button at the end of the screen's toolbar fills the window with the screen; Esc, or the button again, brings the face back. Picture only, on to begin with, hides everything drawn over the trace: the graticule and its labels, the trigger's marks and the cursors, the photocell's reticle, the loop overlay, the hand's mark, and the verdict and readouts. Turned off, they are back, with the panes beside the screen. Two choices are the look's alone, and say so: Which hands, Both, A or B, while a split or a layer draws a figure for each hand, so two figures piled into one cloud can be seen one at a time; and Trail, As heard, Half or Short, which fades the screen faster than the Persistence Scan hears. None of it changes the sound — Scan reads the light each stroke leaves, faded by the Persistence, however the screen is drawn — none of it is a step in undo, and the page forgets it when it closes. Opening and closing redraw the screen from blank; the light Scan reads is kept.
  • The face and Settings The strip along the top keeps the preset, and the Picture section along the bottom of the window is the end of the loop: the Amount, Scan, Strike, Softness and Persistence, Level (the generator's, layer B's while B is on the panel) with the output's meter, the three reads as meters, and Advanced — what Scan reads and the score on one side, the loop overlay, the panes and the beam on the other, which only change the look. The beam's Ink is the figure's colour, the accent or one of five lane inks, and Layer B's ink is the second figure's, its lane's unless you choose (in Y–T each lane keeps its own); Thickness draws the traces thinner or thicker, and Graticule rules the divisions or leaves the screen bare. Scan reads where the light went, not its colour or its width, so none of them changes what you hear. Above the screen are the display (Y–T, X–Y, spectrogram), Clear, Scope & measure — the oscilloscope's own tools in a panel over the screen — run, mode and Autoset; the trigger; the timebase and zoom; the vertical scale, the trace filter, the lanes, the cursors, a saved reference and the readouts under the screen, which are off until you ask for them there. Two of its rows reach the speakers, and are marked so: lag X–Y's Heard and the filter's Speakers get — and Enlarge at the end. The face is the Bench, where everything is played and tuned: the screen on the left, as large as the window allows and still running, and the controls to its right, so you can watch a figure answer with your hand on the control, and the verdict and readouts a line under the screen. On a wide window the Bench stops rather than spreading the columns apart. In a small one the face is compact: the header on one line (the preset's name opens the browser), the tabs without their lines, the modulation cards as chips (as they are in any window under 900 tall), and everything a size smaller. Settings holds what you set once and leave, in two columns — MIDI and This window (whether the help sheet opens the first time, and the Size of everything on the face: Auto is 90 per cent in a window under 1100 by 680 and 100 otherwise, or choose 90, 100 or 125, which this browser remembers); the Input, the Audio device (the site's: in the plugin it is the host's) and Input into the generator. Each section's notes are behind the ⋯ on its title. Saving and sharing sounds is the preset browser's, and the beam's ink is Picture → Advanced. Every section lives in one place and nowhere else. A control with a small gold dot before its name is one the plugin's host can automate: the Picture section's six, the cutoff, the warp, the twist, the delay's and the phaser's mix, and the morph.

    The Bench is three tabs, in the order the sound goes round the loop, each a card with a line under its name of what that stage is doing now, so the face can be read without opening one: Play (the keyboard, the generator, the voice filter), Ink (what the beam draws with: the voice's oscillator, the drawbars, shaping, the drawn cycle), Space & Memory (what the screen does to the drawing: the rack of effects); the picture read back is the Picture section along the bottom.

    The rack is the effects top to bottom in the order the sound goes through them: the Plane, the Phaser, the Chorus, the Delay and, last, the Reverb. Each module is a line with its switch, what it is doing, and its main knobs; its arrow opens the rest of it, one module at a time. The switch turns an effect off by taking its Mix to nought (the Plane's shaping and turn to rest) and back on to what it had, so a setup, a host's knob or a saved code that moves a Mix switches the module with it. The Delay's arrow also holds Tone and Low cut, which are in its loop, so each repeat comes back darker and thinner than the one before; Width, how far apart its repeats are heard, from the diagonal to twice as wide; and Wow, a slow drift of its time, as a tape's speed drifts, so each ghost figure turns a little. Tone takes a modulation source, so a slow LFO can open and close the repeats. The Reverb is a tail of everything before it: Mix and Size (how long it takes to fall away) on its line, and under its arrow Tone, Pre-delay and Spread. At a Spread of nought X and Y go through two reverbs alike, so a held chord keeps its figure and the tail shows only where the sound changes; turned up, each channel has a tail of its own, an ordinary stereo reverb, and the figure clouds over. Past a Mix of a fifth it keeps a held chord moving even in a Settled sound, as the Delay does at full, and its line says so: the screen goes on drawing the tail and the sound goes on reading it. Its switch puts it on below that. Its Mix, Size and Tone take a modulation source, and its Mix is a host parameter. A module that is off folds to its line, and in a window without room for every module's knobs, opening one folds the others to their lines while it is open.

    The phaser, the chorus and the delay can go in any order: drag one by the handle at its left, or give the handle the keyboard and use the up and down arrows, and Escape puts a drag back. The sound changes when you let go. The order is part of the setup and is one for both layers; the plane always comes first, since its turn is the screen's rotation. The plainest difference is the phaser's: before the delay, each repeat keeps the sweep it was played with; after it, the repeats are swept as they come back, together with what you are playing now. Each section's title carries ⋯, and behind it is that section's explanation and the handful of settings reached for rarely.

    The controls on the Bench are knobs. Drag up to turn one up and down to turn it down — the whole range is a short drag, about two centimetres — and hold Shift for a fine turn, a fifth as far. Tap it twice to put it back where the page opened it. A press on a knob gives it the keyboard, so the arrow keys carry on from there. On a phone, a finger on a knob turns it and the page stays put; anywhere else the page scrolls as usual. The number above a knob is its setting; its name, below, lights in the accent as far as the picture is moving it; and a control with something patched on it wears a ring just outside the knob in the selected source's colour, from the setting to as far as that source takes it (backwards for a negative depth), a short tick in its colour for each other source on it, and a dot where the control is right now, all of them together. The pointer is always where your hand set it. Kept as sliders: the drawbars, read across nine at a glance as an organ's are; the setup morph, a crossfader between its two ends; and the strip under the screen, which has width to spare.

    Across the window, under the screen and the tabs, is the modulation row: a card each for LFO 1, LFO 2, the Envelope and the Photocell, each drawing what its source is doing with a dot where it is now, and Routings in the corner. Drag a card onto a knob to put it there; press one to open its editor over the tabs. The picture moves the sound without them. (The microphone and input into the generator are in Settings since 7 November, and the arpeggiator, the clock, the key and tempo and the morph in the Perform menu in the header. The drawings — the harmonograph, the figures, the solids and the second generator — went on 9 November: a setup that had one loads as the waveform.)

    Press / to find any control by name — it knows a few other words for things, so adsr finds the envelope and lfo the oscillators — and choosing a result takes you to it, opening whatever it is behind. The tab is remembered.
  • Modulation Four sources, a card each in the row across the window: two oscillators, the Envelope and the Photocell. The Envelope follows the amp envelope on Play unless its editor says Its own: then it has an attack, decay, sustain and release of its own, opened by the same notes, so a filter or the picture can swell on other timings than the loudness. It is one envelope for all the notes held: on Each phrase a note played while it is open does not start it again, and on Every note each new key starts its attack again from where it is, which on a fast arpeggio twitches. A card draws its source with a dot where it is now — an oscillator's wave, the Envelope's curve, the Photocell's last four seconds — says its rate or reading, and counts the controls it is on; in a small window it is a chip with a small drawing. Press it and its editor opens over the tabs, beside the screen so the picture stays in view: the source drawn large (an oscillator's wave with the dot at its phase and its shape, sync and rate under it; the Envelope's curve, Play's and greyed while it follows Play, with its four times; what the Photocell sees around its reticle, its last four seconds and its value now, On and Place it on the figure), and Where it goes — every control it is on with its own depth and a cross to take it off, and Add a destination to put it on another. A photocell moves a control at most half way, as the picture's sources do. Close, Esc, the card again or a tab puts it away. Pressing a card also selects it: every control it is on draws its ring, and Alt-drag moves its depth.

    Routings, in the row's corner, is every routing in one place, by source or by destination, each with its depth and a cross, and a switch per source that silences its routings and keeps them, to hear the sound without it. A silence is part of the sound: a preset saved, a setup code and the plugin's project keep it with the routings, and undo steps over it. Patching a silenced source switches it back on.

    The keyboard reaches the instrument through Expression, under the Keyboard on Play: the pitch bend's range, and what the mod wheel, pressure and velocity do. Velocity always sets a note's level and how hard it strikes the screen; Level, strike and FM also brightens a note the harder it is struck. What the microphone hears (its pitch, brightness and bands) is parked since 7 November: no card offers it, but a setup that routes one still plays it, and its knob still shows its ink, to be taken off there.

    The Fade, in Routings, is for when modulation should not arrive or leave all at once. In eases it in, Out eases it away, and In and out does both. Under it is the fade's envelope: a wait, the attack, a decay to the level it holds at, the hold, and the release. Drag the end of each stretch sideways for its time; drag the corner where the decay meets the hold up and down for the level held, so a strike can burst and then settle; drag the middle of a slope towards where it is going to make it quick to start, or away to make it slow (or use the arrow keys on a handle). Restart runs the envelope again on every note you strike, and Loop sends the attack and decay round again for as long as a note is held. A dot rides the envelope with the last fade to begin; its height is the level now. With the keyboard split or layered, A and B choose which layer's envelope you are drawing, and the other shows faint behind it: each layer's sound follows its own, and a note struck in a split restarts only its own layer's. The picture's controls follow layer A's. The whole envelope acts on notes; patching or taking off a routing uses its attack and release. It acts on a routing you patch or take off, and on every step the keyboard's sources take: with velocity on the drive, a note starts the drive where it rests and brings it up to how hard you struck, and under Out a release lets it back down slowly. Oscillators, the picture, the envelope and knobs are not eased, because they already move as they should. With any of them on, loading a preset glides its knobs from where they were, so the picture morphs into the new one instead of jumping; its menus and switches still change at once. A depth you drag answers your hand straight away, and a knob you touch during a glide is left where you put it. The fade is kept in this browser and is not part of a setup code, so loading a preset does not turn it off.
  • Morph: one fader, two sounds Morph, in the Perform menu in the header, slides between two sounds. Press A to store every knob, change the sound, press B, and the fader goes between them — the pitch by octaves, everything else in a straight line. Menus and switches are not morphed: a shape or a mode stays as you left it. A knob you turn by hand keeps its place until the fader moves again. The fader is a control like any other, so an oscillator on it moves the whole sound at once. Loading a preset clears it.
  • Hearing: what you play, as sources Parked since 7 November: no card offers these, but a setup that routes one still plays it, so the owner can find out whether they are missed. The Hearing family reads the sound itself, from a microphone, a line input or the generator. Pitch is the note, nought at middle C and one two octaves up, from a held key if there is one and otherwise from the sound; it holds when you stop. Brightness is where the energy sits, low for a dark tone and high for a bright one. Bass, Low mid, High mid and Treble are how loud each band is, at the band split's crossovers. Width is how alike the two channels are, one for mono. Flux jumps on each new note or hit and stays low on a held one. None of them can jump: a new note glides there in an eighth of a second an octave. Pointed back at the generator they are hearing, they are a loop, and held to the picture's reach like the photocell.

    Onset is different: a moment, not a value. It fires once when a note or a hit begins, never on a release, and never faster than twelve times a second, and it can only strike things. What it struck were the drawings' Swing again and Kick, which went with the drawings on 9 November, so for now it strikes nothing.
  • Key, tempo and the quantiser The Key and tempo section, in the Perform menu in the header, is one key, one scale and one tempo for the whole page, with Tap beside the tempo. Where the tempo comes from and the bar are in the Clock section beside it. Quantise the generator's pitch takes the pitch, after everything patched onto it, to the nearest note of the key, so a slow oscillator or the photocell on the frequency plays a melody in D dorian rather than a siren. A key you play outside the scale is moved too, and a note exactly between two goes down. It waits a tenth of a semitone past half-way before it steps, and never steps more than forty times a second, so a pitch resting between two notes does not flicker. Glide, behind the section's ⋯, slides between steps.

    An oscillator's Sync locks its rate to the tempo in note values, from four bars to a semiquaver, with triplets. Tap sets the tempo from the last four taps and starts the locked oscillators on the beat you tapped. A keyboard or sequencer sending MIDI clock sets the tempo while it runs, and hands it back half a second after it stops. Its Start restarts the locked oscillators, and Continue does not.

    Bar says where the page is in the music, in fours: 3.2 is the third bar's second beat. The score's playhead reads its columns from it, so switched on mid-bar it joins where the bar is, and its first column always lands on a downbeat. Stop holds the bar and silences the score; Start puts the bar back to the one and restarts the locked oscillators with it, so a synced sweep and the score begin together. While it runs, a tap is the one as well as the tempo. A device's Start, Stop and Continue work the bar the same way - Start on the device's first tick, as MIDI says it should - and while its clock runs the bar counts its ticks, so it keeps the device's place and not only its tempo. If the clock stops without a Stop, the bar carries on from where the clock would have had it. Two things do not follow the bar: the arpeggiator, which starts from your hands, because a first note held back to the next step would feel like lag; and a song position from the device, which is not read, so a Continue from the middle of a song carries on from wherever this page's bar stood.
  • The trigger is what makes the trace stand still. Without it every frame starts at a different point of the wave and the picture scrolls.
  • Level and edge The scope waits for the signal to cross this value going that way, and starts drawing there. The dashed rose line is the level.
  • Position puts the window before the edge At 10% you see a tenth of the screen's worth of what happened before the trigger. The marker at the top is where t = 0.
  • Holdoff rejects an edge with another close behind it Which settles a waveform that crosses the level more than once a cycle. Stated as a quiet interval before an edge rather than a lockout after one, because this redraws a sliding buffer rather than sweeping once per trigger.
  • Auto, Normal, Single Auto draws whatever arrived, triggered or not. Normal holds the last triggered frame rather than showing an untriggered one. Single arms, catches one edge and stops — which is how you catch a transient.
  • Free run is not a fault When nothing crosses the level the trace goes grey and keeps moving. A signal with no edge in it is silence, not an error. Rust is kept for what wants your attention — clipping, a level over, an input that would not open, a scope stopped or muted — and free run is never one of them.
  • Autoset Reads the signal and picks a timebase, a level and a vertical scale that fit it. It is in Scope & measure, above the screen.
  • Everything the scope can tell you about the signal is along the bottom, one row per channel.
  • The numbers Peak and RMS in dBFS, peak-to-peak, frequency, period, the nearest note, duty cycle, and total harmonic distortion. fs is the level that reaches the top of the graticule.

    The frequency is the sound's period: the shortest time after which the wave nearly repeats itself, however many times it crosses the middle on the way. So a rich registration or a harmonic-heavy organ reads its note, and a sound built from the second and third harmonics alone reads the fundamental it is missing. It needs two periods on screen; with fewer, or with nothing periodic there, it shows a dash rather than a guess. The tuner, the X–Y ratio, Autoset and the automatic lag all read the same number.
  • They are about the signal, not about the picture Full scale and zoom are where the trace sits and how big it is, and neither touches a number here. The screen's rotation, the Plane's Turn, is the one shared transform that does reach the samples — on a stereo pair it turns the lanes themselves, and the speakers with them — so these numbers read the signal as it arrived unless you say otherwise. Numbers read → Turned, in Scope & measure under Measure, points them at what is on the screen instead, and the readout says post-rotation so you can tell. The level meter and the Clipping verdict stay on the signal either way.
  • Cursors are draggable Turn them on in Scope & measure, above the screen. Two in time and two in amplitude, on the Y–T display; the readout gives the difference between each pair, and Δt as a frequency.
  • The longest timebase depends on the converter The scope reads its history out of an analyser, and Web Audio caps one at 32768 samples — 743 ms at 44.1 kHz, but only 341 at 96, because that cap is a count of samples rather than a length of time. So the slowest sweeps are available on one machine and not on another, and the timebase says past the buffer rather than leaving you to notice a trace that stops early. The readout gives the shortfall in milliseconds when it happens.
  • THD only answers when there is a tone It needs a real spectral line — a local maximum standing well above the band. Noise is all peaks, so it says nothing rather than inventing a number.
  • The harmonics pane The fundamental in ink and its partials beside it. A square wave shows odd harmonics tall and even ones almost absent, and about 41% distortion — the first eight partials' worth, which is what this counts. The generator's own waveforms are band-limited, so what you are reading is the waveform rather than the arithmetic that drew it.
  • A reference trace Save reference, in Scope & measure, freezes what is on screen and keeps it dashed behind the live trace, so you can see what changed.
  • The goniometer Left against right, turned 45°. Upright is mono, a circle is wide, and horizontal means the two channels are fighting each other.
  • Two sources, and a generator with four minds of its own. Settings → Input.
  • Tone or Mic The tone is arithmetic, and runs the moment the page opens. Mic asks the browser for your input, a microphone or a line input, and draws it; X–Y draws its left against its right. There is no file player: a keyboard is what plays the generator, and inside the plugin the host plays the track and the plugin draws what it is given.
  • Playing live: split the input into bands Under Mic, Split → Into bands puts what you are playing through four crossovers. One instrument down one input becomes four lanes, and low end against upper harmonics is an X–Y figure that moves because you moved. Four filters, and honest about it — a kick and a hi-hat land in different lanes because they are at different frequencies, not because anything worked out that one is a drum. Picture → Lanes solos, mutes and lays them out. The browser's echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain are all turned off: they are built for voice calls and every one of them reshapes the waveform you came here to look at.
  • Microphone or line, and what may be heard A microphone is never sent to the speakers, because what comes out of them goes straight back into it. A line input — a keyboard, an interface, a mixer's output — has no ear, so there is no loop to make, and it can be monitored through the page behind an explicit toggle. Which one is plugged in is something you assert and the browser cannot check, so wear headphones the first time you turn it on.

    The cost is latency: what you hear has been through the converter and the page's buffers, which is tens of milliseconds and enough for a keyboard player to feel. The reading beside the toggle is the browser's own figure for the output side, so treat it as a floor. Hearing the instrument directly and letting this page only look is the version with no delay in it at all.
  • Four bands, one timebase, one trigger Lanes on different timebases cannot be compared, which is the only reason to stack them, so there is one. One lane provides the edge and every lane is cut at that index — pick which under Trigger → Source. It is how a four-channel bench scope works, for the same reason.
  • Stacked or overlaid Stacked gives each band its own strip and its own name, and answers what is each part doing. Overlaid puts them on one graticule and answers how do they line up. Press Autoset on the bands and each lane is scaled to its own level, which is what makes the treble visible under the bass at all.
  • X–Y across two bands Not just left against right: the bass band against the treble says where the energy of a note goes as it rings. The goniometer follows the same pair.
  • The generator is always heard What the generator draws goes to the speakers, from the first press that lets the browser make a sound; there is no switch. It used to be off when the page opened, as an instrument for looking at signals; but the picture and the sound are one instrument, and a silent generator was half of it. Its level is how to quiet it. It plays in the audio thread and out through the same chain a line input gets — so the filter, the AC coupling and the rotation (the Plane's Turn) shape what you hear as well as what you see, whenever Speakers get is on Shaped. The trace is the waveform that went to the speakers, sample for sample, rather than a second run of the same arithmetic. It runs compiled, as WebAssembly — the same code the plugin plays — and so do the effects on a live input and the photocell and what the picture says; a browser that will not load it gets the page's own JavaScript, which sounds and draws the same, and ?core=js on the address asks for that one.
  • The whole instrument, compiled — and ?brain=js What you are playing is the instrument the plugin is: its brain and its sound, compiled, playing in the audio thread, with this page as its face. Your notes, controls, presets and drawings reach it, its notes go out of your MIDI port, and the picture is the one it drew. The browser lets it be heard only once you have pressed something, and the line under the title says so until then; meanwhile the same instrument draws on the page's own thread, so the screen is never blank. With no keyboard plugged in and the screen's keys shut it draws its generator at once; the waveform waits for a note only once there is something to play one on. Every source is its: Mic is drawn through its plane effects and heard only if it is a line input you have asked to hear; Into bands is its own. ?brain=js on the address is the way back: the page's own brain, written in JavaScript, driving the compiled sound, as the site played before. It stays because the compiled instrument is checked against it, sample for sample. The oscillators that move the picture - the trigger, the filter, the zoom - are the instrument's own, so one routed to the picture and the sound moves them together, on the site and inside the plugin alike.
  • The envelope, and when it is in force Only while a keyboard is playing. With nothing plugged in the amplitude is its knob and nothing else, exactly as it always was. Where the gate is open with no key down, the readout says gated · no note held rather than leaving you to wonder.

    A second key over a held one changes the pitch without starting the envelope again, which is what makes a run of notes a phrase; glide slides between them, and in Poly each new note slides from the last one's pitch. Envelope is also a source — send it to the rotation and the figure opens as the note does. It is not the same thing as Level, which measures whatever is being drawn rather than following a key.
  • Waveform Sine, square, pulse, triangle, saw, four noises, a sine with a third harmonic, drawbars, morph, a cycle you draw and a wavetable of four. The interval sets the right channel against the left.

    Pulse is a square whose Width you set, 5 to 95 per cent: at a half it is the square, and narrower it grows thinner and more nasal, losing the harmonics at multiples of one over its width - a quarter has no fourth or eighth. Put an oscillator on Pulse width and it moves: pulse-width modulation, the slow shimmer of every analogue string pad.

    The noises: white is every frequency alike, a hiss; pink falls 3 dB an octave, so every octave carries the same power, like rain; brown falls 6, a rumble like surf. Stepped is sample and hold: a new random level every cycle of the note, held until the next, so it is noise with a pitch - the trace a staircase, the spectrum a hole at the note and every harmonic. For a supersaw, put the saw through Unison with some Spread.

    Drawn cycle is one period of the wave, drawn with the pointer in the pane on the Ink tab: whatever you draw is what you hear, and what the trace shows. Sine starts again and Smooth rounds the corners. Grab takes one cycle of what is playing instead: choose Mic, play a note into it, hold the same note on the keyboard, press it, and the generator plays that sound's cycle under your hands. Without a note held the pitch is measured, and the reading beside the button says which. It keeps every harmonic under the top of the audible range at any pitch, so a sharp drawing is bright low down and gentler high up, as a real instrument is, and never gains the whistles a naive wavetable does.

    Wavetable is four drawn cycles and a Position that slides between them, 1 to 4, crossfading the two either side - put an oscillator or the pedal on it and the timbre travels. It starts as a sine, an organ's three partials, a saw and a narrow pulse; the switch on the pane chooses which one you draw, and Grab fills the one chosen, so four sounds you played can be four places round the knob.

    Morph is one knob through sine, triangle, saw and square, crossfading between each pair, so the shape is something a source can move: put an oscillator, the pedal or the photocell on it and the timbre changes as you play. On a whole station it is exactly that shape. Its saw is the menu's half a cycle later, so the note does not thin out on the way from the triangle to the saw, as it would with the saw's fundamental upside down against the triangle's. Full depth on it is a station and a half either way.

    Drawbars are the organ's way of making a sound: nine sine partials at the footages of a tonewheel organ, each drawn from nought to eight on the Ink tab. 8′ is the note; 16′ is an octave under it and 5⅓′ a fifth above that, and the rest are the octaves, fifths and third above. Each step is about three decibels, as on the organ, and however many bars are out the wave stays inside the amplitude, so pulling more out changes the colour and not the level. With the drawbars chosen, the registration shows under the Shape menu — 00 8740 000 to start — and pressing it goes to the bars. Every bar is a destination: put an oscillator on one. In X–Y at an interval the figure shows how the partials line up.

    A registration with the 16′ out, such as 88 8000 000, has a cycle twice the note's, and the readout's frequency is the sound's rather than the key's: an octave under. At 1 ms/div the screen holds less than two of those cycles, and the readout says nothing rather than guess. The tuner can read the key instead: with a keyboard, tick take the lag and the tuner from the note played, under Vertical in Scope & measure.
  • Intervals draw consonance A figure closes when the two frequencies are a ratio of small whole numbers, which is what a consonant interval is. In just tuning a fifth is exactly 2:3 and stands still; in equal it is slightly off, and the figure turns at the rate the interval beats.
  • Play it: a MIDI keyboard Settings → MIDI → Connect. Two held notes become the two channels, so the interval under your hands is the figure on the screen: hold a fifth and 2:3 stands still, walk through thirds and the figure walks with you. The lower note goes on X and the higher on Y whichever finger landed first, so the picture turns only when the interval does. A third note takes the place of the older of the two. Mono instead takes the newest note as the pitch and leaves the interval to the menu; Hold keeps the last interval above a single note, which is how you walk a figure up a melody with one finger.

    Poly sounds every note you hold, up to eight, each with its own envelope, on the waveform generator. A chord has more notes than the screen has axes, so Draw chooses its outline: the lowest of the chosen notes leans onto X and the others onto Y, and by default they are the bass and the melody — over comping, the line against the bass. Lowest, highest and most recent are the other choices, two to eight notes of them. Every other note is drawn too, in the middle along the diagonal, and what you hear is exactly what is drawn: a leaning note is louder on its side and still in both ears. The readout says how many make the outline: outline 2 of 5 notes, and what interval that outline is and how fast it turns: fifth, turning 0.74 a second. A chord draws the same figure however you got to it — a note added to keys already held starts in step with them, as if the chord had been struck at once — so a chord you know is a picture you know. Each key sounds at its own pitch. Tune a chord to its lowest note, under the section's extra controls, makes a major triad exactly 4:5:6 so its figure closes — at the price that every note moves a few cents depending on what is under it, which is what just tuning a chord means. A chord is louder than a note; the limiter catches it.

    Tuning applies to what you play: just snaps the interval to its whole-number ratio and the figure stands still, equal takes the keys as they are and it turns at the rate the interval beats. A tempered fifth turns about three quarters of a time a second, which is worth seeing. A tempered third turns nearly nine times a second, which under persistence is a blur. The readout names the interval and says which: fifth, still or major third, turning 8.73 a second, and with Layers split, each layer's outline.

    A note is also the only pitch here that is not estimated, so the lag, the tuner and the timebase can be told to take it as read — no confidence gate, no second of settling. The tuner then reads the gap between the key you pressed and the pitch that came back, which on an organ is a real number rather than an error.

    A sustain pedal works as a pedal does: keys let go while it is down go on sounding until it lifts, and a key struck again under it and still held stays when it does. The notes it is holding are held from the moment it passes half-way, as the MIDI specification has it for a switch.

    Pitch bend bends every note of both layers, two semitones either way, or up to twenty-four as Pitch bend under Expression says. The mod wheel gives vibrato, a third of a semitone either way at the top, five and a half times a second; Mod wheel can give it to the Picture amount or to Scan's depth instead, or to nothing. Channel pressure (aftertouch, pressing a held key harder) moves nothing unless Pressure gives it somewhere. Velocity always sets a note's level and how hard it strikes the screen, and Velocity can add FM. The four are kept with the setup, under the Keyboard section's ⋯ on Play.

    The swell pedal (controller 11) is the Picture amount. Other knobs and drawbars on the keyboard are not learned since 7 November; in the plugin, the host's MIDI learn reaches its knobs. Web MIDI needs a secure page and permission from whatever embeds it: the published artifact is an iframe that does not grant it, so this works on the GitHub Pages copy and not there, and Safari has no Web MIDI at all.
  • Two layers: a split, or one keyboard twice In Poly, Layers gives the waveform generator a second set of voices. Split sends every note from a key upwards to layer B and the rest to layer A — comping with the left hand, a melody with the right. Press at C4 beside it and play the key B should start from. Layered sends every note to both, so each is two voices at once.

    Edit B turns the generator's panel over to layer B, which has its own shape, level and envelope, its own drawbars and morph, and its own Draw rule, so the comping can draw three notes while the melody draws one. Its pitches are the keys it is given, and the modulation is the generator's — a sweep on the pitch bends both layers. B starts as a copy of A, so a split changes where the notes go and nothing else until you change it.

    The Plane module in the rack, on the Space & Memory tab, can give B a plane and a turn of its own; its Layers row says how.

    By default each layer draws its own figure, overlaid: A in the accent and B in olive, and in Y–T as four lanes. A against B draws one figure instead: every note layer A draws on X and every note B draws on Y — the comping against the melody. With a split on, the readout says where, and when a layer is leaving notes out of its outline it says which: outline A 2 of 4, B 1 of 1. While your input is drawn the generator plays one layer: B's picture would have nowhere to go. With a figure each, each figure is also a picture that moves a sound: see Pictures under the picture stage.
  • No keyboard? Keys on the screen Show keys, in the Bench's Play tab, puts two octaves along the bottom of the page, and they play exactly what a MIDI keyboard would — the dyad, Hold, the envelope and the note-as-truth all work from them, and they work in the published artifact and in Safari, where MIDI does not. Drag across them for a glissando. A mouse is one finger, so to hold a dyad tick Tap to hold: each tap then holds its note until tapped again. The computer keyboard plays too, laid out as music software does it — A is C, W C♯, S D and so on along two rows — with Z and X for octaves. While the keys are open those letters play notes rather than their shortcuts; close the keys to have the shortcuts back. Pedal, at the end of the keys, is a sustain pedal that stays down until pressed again, and holding Space while the keys are open is one you hold with your thumb. Closing the keys lifts it. With the keys open the waveform waits for a note, as it does with a keyboard plugged in.
  • Right-click a control — or Ctrl-click on a Mac, hold a finger on it on a touch screen, or press the menu key or Shift+F10 with it focused — and its menu opens beside it, headed with its name and value. First its modulation: each source on it with its depth, which opens the control's editor on that source; then the sources not on it, a press each to add one, and Clear modulation. With nothing on it the list is Modulate with and the four cards' sources. Then its value: Type a value… in the reading's own terms (2k or 2 kHz), Reset with where it starts, and, while the keyboard is split or layered, Copy to layer B (or A). Last, What is this?, its card. A menu or a switch has the same menu without the modulation. The arrows and Enter work in it; Esc or a click away closes it, and nothing in it changes the sound until you choose. The info line says which controls have one.

    The control's editor opens just above the knob, headed with its name and value: a bar of its whole range with your setting marked, each source's sweep as a band in its colour under it and the dot where it is now; then a row per source — its name, which opens its card, a small picture of it moving, a depth that fills out from the middle (left is a minus), a box to type the depth into and a cross to take it off. Pressing a row selects that source. The sources offered are the four modulation cards', and dragging a card straight onto a control is the quick way when you already know where it goes.
  • Changing a depth where it is Alt-drag a knob (Option on a Mac) and it moves the selected source's depth rather than the value; Shift is fine adjustment as on every knob, and Alt with Shift is a fine depth. Or point at the knob and drag the handle at the end of its ring round. While either moves, the reading over the knob and the info line say whose depth and how much — LFO 2 −30%.
  • The lane under a slider is the reading It only reads — there is nothing to aim at. The bar runs from the value you set by hand to where one source takes it, and the tick is where the whole patch has the control at this instant, so a page at rest still shows itself working.

    What the bar draws is the destination's own law, not a fraction of the slider. Full depth on frequency is an octave, so at 220 Hz the bar ends at 440 rather than at the end of a four-kilohertz track. Where a control has a range it cannot leave, a depth that would push past it is kept but the end of the bar dims to say it cannot get there.
  • Several sources on one control They add up, which is how every patch cable ever made behaves. The panel holds as many rows as there are, and the control itself looks and measures exactly the same with one on it or five — the ring and its ticks do the counting, round the outside, and nothing stacks up underneath it. The ring draws one of them: whichever card or editor row you last pressed, or else the first that is there. A depth set to nothing stays patched, because a patch parked at zero is a thing you meant.
  • Point it at the picture Everything here points at anything, whatever the source is. The generator's parameters grey out when there is no generator — a microphone has no interval — but the lag delay, zoom and the filter are the picture's own and take a patch on any input. An oscillator on the plane's Twist turns the figure while you play, which is the difference between a shape that sits there and one that answers.
  • Presets are the front door. Press Preset, on the left of the strip, for a small bank of sounds under two headings, named for what the loop does with a chord you hold. Settled: a note moves the sound as it strikes the screen, and the sound comes to rest while you hold it. Breathing: it keeps moving while you hold it, and stops when you let go, or goes on under the pedal. Each has a line on what to listen for and what to look at. New goes back to the plain sine the instrument opens on, still until you turn Picture up, to start a setup of your own from.
  • Browsing The headings are down the left, each with what it means in a line, and your saved sounds are the last. The middle is the heading's sounds, each with a thumbnail of its figure as the instrument draws it with a note held — a split draws its second hand in layer B's ink — and what to listen for. Choosing one shows it on the right, larger, with what to listen for and what to watch for over the whole of what it says, and loads nothing; Load loads it and leaves the browser open, so you can listen through a heading. Double-click one, or press Enter, to load it and close. The arrows move up and down the list. A heading that grows sections lists them above its sounds, and remembers the one you left it on.
  • What they play on Every one sets the generator, and lands on it wherever it is — the test tone, or under your input. A preset never switches the source: if nothing playing has a generator, the browser says so and offers the test tone.
  • Each one sets everything Including its timebase, because in X–Y the window decides how much of the figure is drawn at once. Anything a preset does not mention goes back to its default, so they cannot leave each other's settings behind.
  • Along the top The preset's name, with its heading above it, between two arrows that step through the bank in the browser's order without opening anything; from a sound that is not one of the bank's, the next is the first. Browse opens the browser, and Save opens it at its save field.
  • Undo The curved arrows undo and redo changes to the sound and the picture, a hundred back: a knob turned, a menu, a preset loaded. A change is one step once it has held still for a moment, so a whole turn of a knob is one, and only a change you made is one — a host's automation moving a knob is not. The history lasts for this session. To compare two sounds, save one, or put them at the morph's two ends.
  • Custom means you have moved off one Nothing is lost; the picker is just telling you the truth.
  • Saving and sharing Along the foot of the browser. Save this sound… asks for a name and keeps the sound you have, with a thumbnail of what it is drawing at that moment (none if nothing is sounding); Delete saved takes away the saved one chosen. Saved sounds live in this browser and nowhere else. The setup code is the whole configuration as text: Copy it to send it, and Paste loads one, from the clipboard or from the field if you paste it there yourself.
  • Keys Space run and stop · S single · A autoset · 1 2 3 Y–T, X–Y, spectrogram · ← → timebase · ↑ ↓ trigger level · + − zoom · C cursors · ? this sheet · Esc back from Enlarge · Ctrl Z undo and Ctrl Shift Z or Ctrl Y redo (⌘ on a Mac). With the on-screen keys open, the letter rows play notes instead: A to ' and W to P, Z X octave, and Space held is the sustain pedal.
